extracted.intended_audience: ICLR 2022 reviewers (program committee reviewers, including new reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural requirements for reviewing submissions to ICLR 2022, including how to read, evaluate, write, discuss, and finalize reviews as well as related administrative actions (bidding, COE reports, conflict handling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely and substantive reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Your reviews are timely and substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews must be submitted within the stated deadlines and should contain substantive assessment rather than brief or perfunctory comments. Timeliness also includes being active and responsive during the discussion phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to reviewing guidelines and Codes
rubrics_metrics.description: You follow the reviewing guidelines below. You adhere to our Code of Ethics in your role as a reviewer. You must also adhere to our Code of Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag any Code of Ethics (CoE) violations and use proper channels for misconduct. Maintain professional conduct and avoid unethical behavior (plagiarism, harassment, undisclosed conflicts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative setup: OpenReview and DBLP
rubrics_metrics.description: Create your OpenReview profile and link your DBLP profile (by September 15th 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping profile information current helps conflict-of-interest detection and proper assignment; failure to do so may increase COI assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bid on papers during bidding window
rubrics_metrics.description: Bid on papers (7 October 2021 - 12 October 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate bidding helps matching algorithms; bid 'Very Low' for papers you have conflicts with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a constructive, thorough and timely review
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a constructive, thorough and timely review (14 October 2021- 1 November 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear, detailed, and helpful. Include summary, strengths, weaknesses, recommendation with reasons, and actionable suggestions to improve the paper. Be generous in tone and specific in critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in discussion phase actively
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss with authors, other reviewers, and ACs to clarify and improve the paper (9 November 2021 - 29 November 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be responsive during discussion (aim to respond within 3 business days). Use discussion to collect additional information, resolve disagreements, and help authors improve their submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a final recommendation by deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a final recommendation to the area chair assigned to the paper (by 29 November 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update your review after discussion and any author revisions; be open to changing your initial recommendation based on new evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging Code of Ethics and policy violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag any potential CoE violations and/or concerns (throughout the review and discussion phase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate CoE violations in the CoE report for the paper; AC/PC/ethics board will handle resolution. For other violations (plagiarism, double submission, formatting), contact AC or PC via official comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the paper carefully and check related work
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the paper: It’s important to carefully read through the entire paper, and to look up any related work and citations that will help you comprehensively evaluate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give yourself sufficient time to understand the submission and its context in the literature; use references to support claims about novelty or correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the paper's objective/goal
rubrics_metrics.description: While reading, consider the following: Objective of the work: What is the goal of the paper? Is it to better address a known application or problem, draw attention to a new application or problem, or to introduce and/or explain a new theoretical finding? A combination of these?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different objectives require different evaluation criteria (e.g., empirical validation for application papers vs. proof/derivation clarity for theory papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess strengths: clarity, correctness, rigor, reproducibility, novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong points: is the submission clear, technically correct, experimentally rigorous, reproducible, does it present novel findings (e.g. theoretically, algorithmically, etc.)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence supporting these claims: complete derivations, comprehensive experiments, code/data or clear instructions for reproducibility, comparisons to baselines, and clearly articulated novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess weaknesses across the same dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak points: is it weak in any of the aspects listed in (strong points)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify where the submission falls short (unclear writing, flawed proofs/analyses, insufficient experiments, missing baselines, lack of reproducibility) and be specific about consequences for claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of reviewer bias; be open-minded to community value
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of potential biases and try to be open-minded about the value and interest a paper can hold for the entire ICLR community, even if it may not be very interesting for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper that seems uninteresting to you personally may still be valuable to others or in future work; avoid letting narrow tastes determine accept/reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer three key questions before recommending
rubrics_metrics.description: Answer three key questions for yourself, to make a recommendation to Accept or Reject: (1) What is the specific question and/or problem tackled by the paper? (2) Is the approach well motivated, including being well-placed in the literature? (3) Does the paper support the claims? This includes determining if results, whether theoretical or empirical, are correct and if they are scientifically rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These core checks should drive your accept/reject judgment; ensure each is supported by evidence or concrete critique in the review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the initial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Write your initial review, organizing it as follows: Summarize what the paper claims to contribute. Be positive and generous. List strong and weak points of the paper. Be as comprehensive as possible. Clearly state your recommendation (accept or reject) with one or two key reasons for this choice. Provide supporting arguments for your recommendation. Ask questions you would like answered by the authors to help you clarify your understanding of the paper and provide the additional evidence you need to be confident in your assessment. Provide additional feedback with the aim to improve the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Followable structure makes reviews easy to navigate for authors and ACs. Use precise, concrete examples (cite sections/tables/figures) and separate 'reason for score' from 'comments for authors'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and concreteness: be polite, precise, constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: General points to consider: Be polite in your review. Ask yourself whether you’d be happy to receive a review like the one you wrote. Be precise and concrete. Provide constructive feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague statements; give concrete suggestions, include references to back up claims, and frame critiques as ways to improve the work rather than attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: State uncertainties explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s also fine to explicitly state where you are uncertain and what you don’t quite understand. The authors may be able to resolve this in their response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark unclear points as questions for authors rather than as definitive flaws when appropriate; this helps focus rebuttal responses and AC decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reject solely for lack of 'interest' or non-SOTA results
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t reject a paper just because you don’t find it 'interesting'. This should not be a criterion at all for accepting/rejecting a paper. Also, if a submission does not achieve state-of-the-art results, that is not by itself grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the paper convincingly demonstrates new, relevant, impactful, or insightful knowledge even if not SOTA; consider theoretical insights, negative results, novel settings, or useful analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the Code of Ethics (CoE) report
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the CoE report: ICLR has adopted the Code of Ethics (CoE). Please check your assigned papers for conflicts with the code of ethics and mark them in your review form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If uncertain about CoE applicability, reach out to your area chair. Use the form provided to document concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary material: optional but useful
rubrics_metrics.description: How should I use supplementary material? It is not necessary to read supplementary material but such material can often answer questions that arise while reading the main paper, so consider looking there before asking authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use supplement to resolve minor missing details; don't force authors to move core claims to supplement to avoid scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting additional experiments: limited and justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Am I allowed to ask for additional experiments? You can ask for additional experiments, but make sure you justify why they’re necessary to push the paper over the acceptance threshold. New experiments should not significantly change the content of the submission. Rather, they should be limited in scope and serve to more thoroughly validate existing results from the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer requests that are feasible in rebuttal (small ablations, clarifying baselines) and clearly explain why they affect the validity of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling other policy violations
rubrics_metrics.description: To flag a CoE violation related to a submission, please indicate it when submitting the CoE report for that paper. The AC will work with the PC and the ethics board to resolve the case. To discuss other violations (e.g. plagiarism, double submission, paper length, formatting, etc.), please contact either the AC or the PC as appropriate. You can do this by sending an official comment with the appropriate readership restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official comment channels; do not attempt to adjudicate serious policy violations yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to contact the Area Chair (AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: How can I contact the AC for a paper? To contact the AC for a paper: (i) go to the OpenReview page for that paper (while being logged into OpenReview); (ii) click the button to add an official comment and fill out the comment form; (iii) add the ACs to the list of 'Readers'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official comments for matters requiring AC attention (COI, major concerns) and set readership appropriately to keep communications private/public as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation expectations for contemporaneous work
rubrics_metrics.description: Are authors expected to cite and compare with very recent work? What about non peer-reviewed (e.g., ArXiv) papers? We consider papers contemporaneous if they are published (available in online proceedings) within the last four months ... authors are not required to compare their own work to that paper. Authors are encouraged to cite and discuss all relevant papers, but they may be excused for not knowing about papers not published in peer-reviewed conference proceedings or journals, which includes papers exclusively available on arXiv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should use judgement; if in doubt, discuss with the area chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest avoidance and handling
rubrics_metrics.description: How can I avoid being assigned papers that present a conflict of interest? Conflicts of interest are detected using your OpenReview profile information (co-authors, past and current institutions, etc.). Therefore, the best way to avoid conflicts of interest is to update your OpenReview profile. If, while bidding, you come across a paper that presents a conflict of interest, please bid 'Very Low' for that paper. If you are assigned a paper that presents a conflict of interest, please contact the program chairs immediately to have that paper re-assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively update profile and bid carefully; promptly report any discovered COI after assignment.
